items.label: text
items.text: This chapter looks at the most common gases in the atmosphere, concentrating on oxygen. We will also look at carbon dioxide, which is a greenhouse gas and may contribute to climate change.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 13.1 Despite the gases added by industry, the air around us is mostly nitrogen and oxygen.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know the approximate percentages by volume of the four most abundant gases in dry air

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand how to determine the percentage by volume of oxygen in air using experiments involving the reactions of metals (e.g. iron) and non-metals (e.g. phosphorus) with air

items.label: list_item
items.text: Describe the combustion of elements in oxygen, including magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur

items.label: list_item
items.text: Describe the formation of carbon dioxide from the thermal decomposition of metal carbonates, including copper(ll) carbonate

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and that increasing amounts in the atmosphere may contribute to climate change

items.label: list_item
items.text: Practical: Determine the approximate percentage by volume of oxygen in air using a metal or a non-metal

items.label: text
items.text: The approximate percentages (by volume) of the four most abundant gases present in unpolluted, dry air are shown in Table 13.1.

items.label: table
items.text:
Table 13.1 Approximate percentages (by volume) of the main gases in unpolluted, dry air

| Gas            |   Amount in air (%) | Amount in air (fraction)   |
|----------------|---------------------|----------------------------|
| nitrogen       |                78.1 | about 4/5                  |
| oxygen         |                21.0 | about 1/5                  |
| argon          |                 0.9 |                            |
| carbon dioxide |                0.04 |                            |

items.label: caption
items.text: Table 13.1 Approximate percentages (by volume) of the main gases in unpolluted, dry air

items.label: text
items.text: There are also very small amounts of the other noble gases in the air.

items.label: text
items.text: It is important to realise that these figures apply only to dry, unpolluted air. Air can have anywhere between 0 and 4% water vapour. The percentage of carbon dioxide in the air, although very small, is rising steadily because of human activity.
